To start, I will test a simple ensemble of the top-performing, diverse models from the error table: THETA, ETS, and rf. This tests if a focused mean of the best individual predictors outperforms broader combinations.

The series is trend-dominated with high trend strength (0.80), suggesting that models capable of capturing or adapting to the trend (like THETA, ETS, ARIMA) are crucial. The current leader used a mean of [ETS, THETA, rf]. RF performed very well in window 0 but poorly in others, indicating instability. A different strategy is to use inverse error weighting on the top-performing models to leverage their relative strengths more dynamically than a simple mean. I will test inverse error weighting on the top 3 models (THETA, ETS, rf) which were already selected in the best attempt, but this time allowing the weights to adjust based on their validation performance.
Testing broad inverse-error weighted combination across all 19 models to leverage diverse signals in a trend-dominated series.

I will also try a trimmed mean on this expanded pool to see if robustness helps against potential outliers or model disagreement in the blind window.

The current leader (a5) uses a trimmed mean on a selective pool (pool5: THETA, ETS, NaiveMovingAverage, ARIMA). To test if a broader, more robust combination of top performers helps, I will try a standard arithmetic mean on the top 4 models by RMSE. This tests if the trimming in the leader is necessary or if simple averaging of the best few is sufficient.

The current leader (trimmed_mean on a selective pool) suggests that robustness against potential outliers or model instability is beneficial, even with low outlier counts. Since the ranking stability is moderate and the series is trend-dominated, testing a strategy that explicitly down-weights less consistent performers using error-trend based weights on the full pool could capture recent performance improvements better than static mean/trimmed_mean. This tests if dynamic weighting adds value over the robust simple combination.

The current leader (trimmed_mean on a small pool of top performers) benefits from removing outliers/noise, which is effective given the high trend strength and non-stationarity. I will test a weighted combination of these three diverse, low-error models using inverse error weighting to see if it captures the trend more effectively than the simple trimmed mean while maintaining stability.
